lead: Timeline animation puts objects on layers and moves a playhead through frames. You set a few keyframes; a motion tween computes frames between them by changing a symbol instance's position, scale, rotation, colour, alpha or filters. Motion blur smears a fast object over the shutter time. Only a few universities teach this advanced topic. It appears in cartoon shorts, app intros and game menus.
prereq: You need: keyframes and interpolation, 2D/3D techniques, and frame rates from Unit 4.

sections.h3: Timeline, layers and two kinds of tween

blocks.text:
The timeline is a grid of frames and layers. Columns are frames numbered from 1. Rows are layers, so independent objects animate without touching each other. A keyframe stores a property value. A blank keyframe is empty, so nothing from the previous frame carries over; you draw or place the new object in it, and the next keyframe stores that object's property values. The playhead marks the frame on screen. Frame rate is frames per second (fps): 24 frames at 24 fps last one second. Use a motion tween for movement and a shape tween for outline morphing.

A motion tween needs a symbol instance. A symbol is a reusable object in the library; an instance is one placement of it on the stage. You set a start keyframe and an end keyframe, and the software computes the frames between. It can tween x and y position, scale, rotation, alpha (opacity), colour tint and filters such as blur. A shape tween instead morphs raw drawing shapes; it does not move a symbol instance.

sections.h3: The tween path, easing and nesting

blocks.text:
The tween path is the route the symbol centre follows. For a straight path, x(t) = x₀ + (x₁ − x₀)t and y(t) = y₀ + (y₁ − y₀)t, where t runs from 0 at the first keyframe to 1 at the last; x₀, y₀ are the start point and x₁, y₁ the end point. Curved paths use Bezier handles.

Easing changes t before interpolation. Ease-in starts slow; ease-out ends slow. The easing curve plots progress against time, so it changes speed along the path.

Swapping the tween target replaces the symbol instance in the keyframes with another library instance. The path and timing remain; only the drawing changes. A nested animation puts a symbol's own inner timeline inside the outer tween: the outer moves the instance while the inner runs a loop, such as a blinking eye. You can tween 3D position along z; perspective changes apparent size with distance, so check the camera convention in your tool (see Unit 2).

Motion blur fakes speed by smearing the object over the time the shutter is open. Shutter angle θ is the open part of 360°; shutter time = (θ ÷ 360°) ÷ fps. A 180° shutter at 24 fps is open for 0.5 ÷ 24 = 1/48 s. Blur length ≈ speed × shutter time: speed is in pixels per second, shutter time in seconds, so blur length is in pixels. A fast object or a long shutter gives a longer smear. A 360° shutter would blur over the whole frame interval. Motion blur is a render or filter effect; it does not change the tween path.

Test the movie at the target frame rate on the phone or projector. A tween that looks smooth at 30 fps may stutter at 24 fps if too much is redrawn. Use the same fps for authoring and playback. Buttons, stop actions, ActionScript and publishing are named only; they are outside this unit's scope.

examples.question: A symbol tweens from x = 100 px to x = 400 px over 24 frames at 24 fps. Find average speed and motion blur length with a 1/48 s shutter.
examples.answer: Duration 1 s, average speed 300 px/s, blur length 6.25 px.
examples.check:
frames = 24
fps = 24
x0 = 100
x1 = 400
shutter = 1 / 48
duration = frames / fps
speed = (x1 - x0) / duration
blur = speed * shutter
print(duration)
print(speed)
print(blur)

traps: Putting a motion tween on a raw shape: it needs a symbol instance; shape tween is for raw shapes.
Reporting tween length in frames when asked for seconds: divide frames by fps.
Confusing shutter angle with shutter time: shutter time = (θ ÷ 360°) ÷ fps.
Using distance as blur length: blur length = speed × shutter time.

quiz.a: A frame storing a property value; tweens fill between keyframes.

quiz.q: What does a motion tween animate?
quiz.a: A symbol instance's position, scale, rotation, alpha, colour or filters.
It smears a fast object over the shutter time, so speed reads clearly.

quiz.q: A 60-frame tween plays at 30 fps. Duration?
Object moves 50 px to 250 px in 20 frames at 20 fps; shutter 1/40 s. Speed and blur?
quiz.a: Duration 1 s; distance 200 px; speed 200 px/s; blur 200 × 1/40 = 5 px.

quiz.q: Linear versus ease-in tween: compare blur across the tween.
quiz.a: Average speed and total duration are the same for both. In an ease-in the object moves slowly at the start and quickly near the end, so blur is short in the early frames and longest near the last frames. A linear tween gives the same blur on every frame, blur = average speed × shutter time. At the exact mid-time the ease-in value may be below, equal to or just above the linear value depending on the easing curve, so do not claim 'shorter' without fixing the curve.

beyond: Not for the exam. CSS transforms and the Web Animations API use the same keyframe-and-easing model. Lottie exports timeline tweens to JSON for mobile apps. Game engines use motion vectors for post-process blur. Search: motion tween, shutter angle, motion vectors, Lottie.
